%% The two wide tables run in landscape. pdflscape rather than lscape so the PDF
%% carries a /Rotate on those pages and a viewer shows them the right way up
%% without the reader turning their head. Inside the environment \textwidth
%% becomes the portrait \textheight, so the block goes from 182 mm to 261 mm --
%% which is what makes a ten-column table legible instead of a hyphenation stack.
\usepackage{pdflscape}

%% Ragged-right p column. Justifying a 25 mm column stretches interword space and
%% forces two or three hyphenations per line; ragged right is what a dense table
%% actually wants. \arraybackslash restores \\ after the > directive eats it.
\newcolumntype{L}[1]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{#1}}

\title{\vspace{-1.5em}One Hundred Sixty-one Candidates for Datasets 51--200}
\author{Michael Volk}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\thispagestyle{empty}

\noindent
The database holds 50 schematized and L0--L4-verified \org{Saccharomyces cerevisiae}
datasets, of which 36 are served and 14 are built and waiting on the next full graph
rebuild. Reaching 200 needs 150 more. Table~\ref{tab:candidates} ranks 161 candidates and
Table~\ref{tab:sources} gives each one's citation, link and data location.

The list is ordered for a decision about the next build week rather than for the
long-run total, so it carries two near lines as well as the arithmetic one. Rows 1--50 are
the recommended next builds, rows 51--70 are the bench behind them, and rows 71--150
complete the set that reaches 200. Ranking puts the rows a planned yeast Perturb-seq is
designed against first, then the rows that place metabolism and expression on genotypes
that can be joined, then scale (Sec.~\ref{sec:rule}). Table~\ref{tab:synergies} names every
join a candidate opens, against a supported dataset or against another candidate, with the
shared axis that makes the pair addressable. Table~\ref{tab:swaps} records every rank
change against the previous pass. Table~\ref{tab:excluded} records what was considered and
dropped, which is where the one hard constraint shows up: a dataset earns a place only if
the total genomic content of each strain can be reconstructed.
